C01.why: Controls are minimal (stick + one Interact/Report), but the core skill (noticing what changed versus a remembered 'normal' and then sorting it into one of 4 abstract categories) is cognitively heavy for 8-10 year olds. Day/night phases, nerve pips, roles and CCTV add to it, and the horror tone may put off the youngest.
C01.fix: Drop the category pick (tap the anomaly and it's reported), and give a 'how it should look' snapshot button on night 1 so spotting becomes spot-the-difference rather than memory.

C02.why: Keep Talking-style information asymmetry is among the hardest designs for kids: the Book role means reading and applying rule logic, players have to relay it through an 8-icon wheel with no chat, roles rotate every 90 seconds, and strangers fill the team. Without verbal help, most 8-12 year olds will fail the first several rounds without knowing why.
C02.fix: Make rule pages fully pictographic (symbol → colour → action, no text), and start with a solo or 2-player one-module device as an interactive tutorial before the 3-role mode unlocks.

C03.why: One hold button and an auto camera, with an obvious goal (get down the river, don't go over the waterfall), so it reads within seconds and the chaos is fun even before players coordinate. The only friction is working out which way your own thruster pushes.
C03.fix: Draw a big coloured thrust arrow from each player's seat that lights up while held, plus a bouncing arrow toward the next checkpoint.

C04.why: The theme is approachable, but the loop asks kids to compare items with a reference catalogue, find subtle 'tells', use three tools and set prices on an offer slider. That means reading, careful attention and economic reasoning, and the forger PvP adds deception on top.
C04.fix: Replace the offer slider with Buy/Reject, make tells glow once the right tool passes over them, and show the catalogue as a side-by-side picture match with no text.

C05.why: Kids grasp the fantasy instantly ('make a mess, hide it before Mom gets home'), each phase explains itself through visible events (the car in the driveway), and controls are stick + Grab/Throw + Jump. The Parent role and the score math (Fun − Evidence) are slightly more abstract, and the snitch mechanic adds social complexity.
C05.fix: During PANIC, outline every piece of evidence with a red glow plus a countdown banner, and show a simple 'mess left: 7' counter so the goal of each phase is unmistakable.

C06.why: Tapping hay is immediate and the tycoon/incremental loop is familiar to Roblox kids, but placing conveyor → sifter → magnet chains on a grid assumes some grasp of automation. The 'find 24 needles in a shared pile' goal is abstract and the payoff is slow.
C06.fix: Guide the first machine with a pulsing arrow ('Place your first sifter here') and show a giant server-wide 'Needles found: 3/24' meter with each needle's glint visible in the pile.

C07.why: The objective (climb up together) is obvious and there are only three buttons. But physics climbing with stamina, cold, carry weight and an anchor timing mechanic tends to frustrate younger players on mobile, and one child's mistake drags down the whole team.
C07.fix: Add a forgiving 'auto-grab' on near-misses and make Anchor a big context-sensitive button that only appears (and pulses) when a teammate is falling.

C08.why: 'Film the ghosts' is a clear, funny fantasy with simple controls, but the scoring feedback is delayed (you only learn what earned views after 6 minutes, in the montage), so kids won't know what 'good footage' means during play. The horror tone also narrows the youngest audience.
C08.fix: Show a live 'views' counter and a 'SPOOKY SHOT! +500' pop-up on the camera HUD the moment a ghost event is in frame.

C09.why: Drawing shapes is natural for kids and the goal (defend the tower) is clear, but they have to memorize runes, draw accurately under pressure while also using the thumbstick (hard for small hands on mobile), and learn cross-player combos. Ten-minute sessions are long for this age.
C09.fix: Show translucent rune 'trace guides' on the drawing pad for the 2-3 starter spells, and auto-trigger combos when spells overlap rather than requiring coordination.

C10.why: Creatures appeal to kids, but the stack is complex: roguelite runs, auto-battle placement, upgrade picks, breeding, trait inheritance, mutations and family trees, with trait descriptions that likely require reading. Little of it is understandable in 10 seconds.
C10.fix: Show traits as icons with no text and hide breeding until after the first completed run; make the first run a fixed, guided 3-battle tutorial.

C11.why: 'Grab stuff and get out before the monster catches you' is graspable, but noise-based hunting, carry slowdown, contracts and losing your haul on failure are extraction-genre concepts that confuse and frustrate younger players. The concept is underspecified on UI and onboarding.
C11.fix: Add an always-visible noise meter (ear icon filling up) and a glowing exit beacon, and let kids keep 1 artifact even on failure.

C12.why: Three distinct control schemes (tilt stick, tap panels, map pings) plus asymmetric information that has to be relayed through pings alone is a lot for kids without voice. The emergencies and landing need understanding of a plane's systems, and the concept is underspecified on onboarding.
C12.fix: Make every emergency a single big flashing icon visible to all roles, with the fix being 'engineer taps the matching flashing panel'; auto-stabilize the pilot so only steering matters.

C13.why: Grand-strategy concepts (sending a percentage of troops, cities and ports, alliances, betrayal) on a 50-player map are opaque to 8-12 year olds. OpenFront-style play requires reading the map and economic reasoning, and new players get eliminated quickly without understanding why.
C13.fix: Use a bot-only practice map with a one-tap 'expand' button and a large arrow to the nearest free land, and replace troop percentages with fixed small/medium/all buttons.

C14.why: Delivering a fragile parcel without breaking it is intuitive, and the floating value meter that drops on bumps is excellent, instantly readable feedback. The multi-phase loop (accept, load, drive with pedals, carry, two-person carry) means kids must learn on-foot plus vehicle controls.
C14.fix: Make the driving segment optional or auto-drive with simple left/right steering only, and show a big arrow to the customer's door.

C15.why: Drag-and-drop and merge-three are familiar from mobile merge games, but auto-battler strategy (board placement, synergies, why you lost) is opaque. A 30-second draft timer with 8 players adds pressure, and elimination math is hard to follow.
C15.fix: Show a simple 'your army power vs. theirs' bar before each fight and add an 'auto-place' button so kids can't lose purely to placement confusion.

C16.why: Taking care of pets before the owners return is a theme kids understand instantly, and chores-plus-chaos is self-explanatory. The concept is badly underspecified, though (no controls, UI or multiplayer described), so the score rests on the theme alone.
C16.fix: Specify the controls (stick + one Interact) and show need bubbles above each pet (food bowl, bath, ball icons) so kids know what to do without any text.

C17.why: Stacking blocks up to a height line is universally intuitive and the controls are simple. But turn-taking means waiting, rotation and placement precision with touch can frustrate, and physics collapses caused by teammates can feel unfair to young players.
C17.fix: Show a ghost preview of where the piece will land, and a stability wobble indicator before release.

C18.why: Raising one big monster is appealing, but the loop is vague (gather, vote, train), the payoff comes once a week on Saturday, and a child joining midweek won't see how their actions matter. The concept is badly underspecified.
C18.fix: Give every contribution an instant visible effect on the monster (it grows or eats on screen), and run mini practice fights every 10 minutes so the payoff isn't a week away.

C19.why: It builds on Red Light Green Light, which every child already knows: move when the light is away, freeze when it finds you. Two buttons and a visible beam make it readable in seconds, and the pranks are funny. Telling yourself apart from 30 NPC statues and spotting prank targets may need some guidance.
C19.fix: Give prank targets a sparkle outline and show a big 'FREEZE!' screen-edge warning when the beam is near; give the Guard a simple 'tags left: 3' badge.

C20.why: One input (tap where the ball goes) and a sport kids know make it readable in seconds. But the pitch is underspecified: player movement, timing windows and positioning aren't described, and the ranked competitive framing is less forgiving for young players.
C20.fix: Add a landing-shadow marker for the incoming ball and a forgiving timing window with an 'auto-run to ball' default, so tapping is the only skill needed.

overall_notes: Strongest for kids: concepts built on fantasies or games children already know (Red Light Green Light, a messy house before Mom gets home, a raft down a river, stacking blocks) with 1-2 buttons. Weakest: concepts that rely on reading, information asymmetry relayed only through emotes (C02, C12), or strategy and economic reasoning (C13, C10, C04). Because chat is gated by age check, any design that needs players to pass information to each other is much harder for under-13s. Several concepts (C11, C12, C16, C18, C20) are too underspecified on UI and onboarding to score with confidence. Horror concepts (C01, C08, C11) are understandable but narrow the youngest end of the 8-12 range.
